newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Austrian becomes McDonald's burger king.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Austrian becomes McDonald's burger king.

text.p: It's a long climb up the McDonald's career ladder from serving French fries in Vienna to becoming the first non-American on the burger chain's Chicago-based global board.
Austrian-born Andreas Hacker, 41, made it in 20 years.
Hacker, appointed to the global board in June, joined McDonald's first outlet in Austria as a part-time crew member in 1977 while studying economics at Vienna University.
"The McDonald's at Schwarzenbergplatz was really the place to go in '77," said Hacker in an interview. "You could meet all the actors, politicians, sports people."
Hacker's first promotion came just four weeks later when he was made responsible for the kitchen area.
By 1984, he was director, McDonald's Austria.

"We had 12 restaurants in those days -- not a real big deal," he recalls. After a period with McDonald's Germany, Hacker returned to his home country in 1990 and became managing director, Central Europe and Austria in 1992.

Under his stewardship, Austrian turnover rose to nearly 2.7 billion schillings ($217.6 million) in 1996 from 756 million in 1990. Austria is one of the five most profitable McDonald's subsidiaries in the world.
Every minute another 18 Big Macs and 43 portions of French fries are ordered somewhere within Austria's 85 branches, according to company statistics.
And around 50 Austrian milk farmers owe their livelihoods to the "Shake" and "McSundae", the company says.
ROOM FOR GROWTH ACROSS EUROPE
Hacker insists there is room for growth in Western Europe, saying only 85 of Austria's 35,000 restaurants and snack-bars are McDonald's.
Central Europe has seen expansion. There are 205 restaurants across 13 countries in central Europe, with plans for nearly 800 more by the year 2000.
Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan should see their first McDonald's open within the next three years.
Hacker, who now also carries a German passport, sees a natural post-Habsburg affinity between the Austrians and their eastern neighbours.

"I think these people are the smartest, most intelligent and most aggressive I've ever seen," Hacker says. "Take the Hungarians. They always had this business mentality. They come to Vienna, buy a dishwasher, take it home and sell it and then come back."

Hacker himself has a Polish mother, Bavarian father, Russian grandmother and Austrian wife. He offers to speak in various European languages and the name-plate on his desk is written in cyrillic script.
"I feel at home where my bed is," he says. "You could move me to Singapore tomorrow and I'd feel at home there."
Appointed corporate vice president on the global board, Hacker keeps responsibility for central Europe and Austria, but will take a view on the company's affairs world wide.
"I still know how to assemble a shake machine," says Hacker, who believes his first-hand experience of the company at all levels has earned him respect.
He says he personally spent two and a half years choosing staff for McDonald's in Vienna, right down to the receptionists at the company's World Trade Centre Austrian headquarters.
"It's hard to replace a good receptionist -- it's easy to replace a member of the board," he said. ($ = 12.40 Austrian Schillings)
